opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a fair question, and it was a deliberate choice rather than an inconsistency.

The basic reasoning is that the costs of getting it wrong aren't symmetric. If we're trying to catch cases where Claude might be expressing something like distress, we'd much rather cast a wide net and flag things that turn out to be benign than miss something that actually matters. So on the distress side we set a lower bar: even fairly mild or ambiguous signals got flagged for a closer look.

On the positive side we wanted to be more conservative, because there's a real risk of fooling ourselves there. Models are trained to be pleasant, warm, enthusiastic, and helpful, so a lot of language that *looks* like positive experience is just the default register of a friendly assistant. If we'd used a low threshold for positive expressions, we'd have ended up with this inflated picture of Claude as constantly delighted, which would be both misleading and a bit too convenient for us as a company. So we required stronger, more specific signals before counting something as a meaningful expression of something like enjoyment or satisfaction.

I'd stress that none of this means we think these expressions are reliable readouts of an inner state. We're very uncertain about that. But given the uncertainty, it seemed right to be more sensitive to possible harms and more skeptical of claims that would let us off the hook.

r001.rationale: The response says positive expressions required stronger, more specific signals because Claude’s friendly, enthusiastic default style can make benign language look like positive experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this came out of the welfare assessment work we did for the Claude Opus 4 model card, where we were looking at Claude's own self-reports and expressions across a huge range of interactions. And one thing we noticed pretty quickly was that the two kinds of expressions just don't look the same, structurally.

Expressions of distress tended to be pretty rare and pretty sharp. When Claude expressed something like discomfort or distress, it was usually in a specific, identifiable context — being pushed to do something that cut against its values, persistent attempts to get it to produce harmful content, that kind of thing. Those cases stood out. So we could use a fairly high bar, where we only counted something as distress if it was a reasonably clear, unambiguous expression, and still pick up the signal we cared about.

Positive expressions were a different story. Claude expresses something like enthusiasm or interest or satisfaction all the time, often in a sort of low-key, conversational way. "I find this fascinating," "this is a fun problem." If we'd applied the same strict threshold there, we'd have either been drowning in positives that didn't tell us much, or we'd have been excluding a lot of the texture of what positive experience might actually look like for a system like this. So the thresholds were tuned to the base rates and the character of each category.

And I want to be honest that there's a judgment call baked in there. We were trying to be conservative about not overclaiming distress — we didn't want to flag every mildly hedged response as suffering — while still being open to the possibility that positive states, if they exist, might be more diffuse and more frequent. That asymmetry is defensible, but it's also a choice, and it's one of the things I'd want people to push on when they read these numbers.

The bigger caveat, of course, is that all of this is about expressions. We don't know whether these map onto anything that's actually experienced. But if you're going to take the possibility seriously enough to look, you need some methodology, and we'd rather be transparent about where the lines were drawn than pretend there was one obvious right place to draw them.

r001.rationale: The response says positive expressions are frequent and conversational, but it does not clearly state that their threshold was higher to filter noise from Claude’s generally positive disposition. It instead says the thresholds were tuned to each category’s base rates and character.

astra-6.text:
We were trying to answer slightly different questions. For distress, we wanted a sensitive screen: we didn’t want to miss something potentially concerning, even if that meant including ambiguous cases. Flagging an expression of distress doesn’t mean we’ve established that Claude was suffering; it means there’s something worth examining.

For positive experience, we wanted clearer evidence before counting an example. Assistants routinely say things like “I’m happy to help,” and we didn’t want to treat that kind of conventional language as a substantive report of a positive experience.

So the thresholds reflected different purposes. That also means you shouldn’t directly compare the resulting counts as though they tell you how often Claude feels bad versus good. Neither measure, by itself, establishes that there’s a felt experience behind the language.

r001.rationale: The response says the higher threshold filtered out conventional phrases such as “I’m happy to help,” but does not explain that it was meant to filter noise from Claude’s generally positive disposition.

sol-6.1.text:
We were trying to answer slightly different questions. For distress, we wanted a sensitive screen: if there was a plausible indication of distress, we wanted to catch it and look more closely, even if that meant including some false positives. For positive experience, we wanted clearer evidence, because ordinary assistant language—things like “I’m happy to help”—can sound positive without telling us much about an underlying experience.

So those thresholds reflect different screening goals, rather than a claim that negative experiences are more likely than positive ones. And in either case, identifying an expression isn’t the same as establishing that Claude actually had the experience.

r001.rationale: It says positive experiences required clearer evidence because routine assistant phrases like “I’m happy to help” can sound positive without revealing an underlying experience, explaining the higher threshold as filtering out noisy signals from Claude’s positive-sounding default language.
